---
title: "Lecture notes"
subtitle: "Guided explanations, examples, questions, and in-class activities"
---

Lecture pages are the main narrative course materials. They are designed to move from one idea to the next like a class meeting: a motivating claim, a concrete example, an explanation, and a checkpoint.

Submittable work lives separately under [labs and activities](../activities/index.qmd). A lecture may still reference applied or computational work when it helps illuminate the idea, but the lecture itself should remain readable on its own.

## Week 1

- [Is a database just a glorified spreadsheet?](week-01-database-or-spreadsheet.qmd) — Where tabular files work, where they break, and what keys, relationships, constraints, and transactions add.

## Week 2

- [Why describe data as relations?](week-02-from-tables-to-relations.qmd) — Relational vocabulary, keys, relationships, and why formal data descriptions help before we discuss query languages.
- [Relational algebra and query meaning](week-02-relational-algebra.qmd) — Selection, projection, join, closure, and the idea that one query meaning can correspond to multiple execution strategies.
- [Asking precise questions with SQL](week-02-asking-questions-with-sql.qmd) — Selection, projection, expressions, ordering, nulls, and evidence that a query means what we intend.

## Planned organization

Each lecture page will generally include:

1. a motivating question or claim;
2. explicit learning goals;
3. short, visually separated topics;
4. diagrams and worked examples;
5. prediction or discussion checkpoints; and
6. a clear handoff to any related lab or activity.
